nodes.name: Convex function
nodes.statement: A function $f$ over a convex domain is convex if for any two points $x$ and $y$ in the domain and any $\lambda \in [0,1]$: $f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y) \leq \lambda f(x) + (1-\lambda) f(y)$. It is concave if the inequality is reversed.

nodes.name: Ranking
nodes.statement: A ranking of a collection of items is a complete, transitive ordering: for every pair $a, b$, either $a > b$ or $b > a$, and $a > b, b > c$ implies $a > c$.

nodes.name: Arrow's axioms
nodes.statement: Three axioms for a global ranking method: (1) Nondictatorship: the algorithm cannot always select one individual's ranking. (2) Unanimity: if every individual prefers $a$ to $b$, the global ranking must prefer $a$ to $b$. (3) Independence of irrelevant alternatives: if individuals keep the order of $a$ and $b$ unchanged, the global order of $a$ and $b$ should not change.

nodes.name: Sparse vector
nodes.statement: A vector $x$ of length $d$ is $s$-sparse if it has at most $s$ nonzero elements, with $s \ll d$.

nodes.name: Incoherence of a matrix
nodes.statement: A matrix $A$ with unit-length columns is incoherent if all pairwise dot products of distinct columns satisfy $|a_i \cdot a_j| < 1/(2s)$ for a given sparsity level $s$.

nodes.name: Hessian matrix
nodes.statement: The Hessian $H(f(x))$ of a function $f$ at $x$ is the symmetric $d \times d$ matrix with $ij$-th entry $\partial^2 f / (\partial x_i \partial x_j)$. The second derivative of $f$ at $x$ in direction $u$ is $u^T H(f(x)) u$.

nodes.name: Semi-definite program
nodes.statement: A semi-definite program (SDP) minimizes a linear function $c^T x$ subject to $F_0 + F_1 x_1 + \cdots + F_d x_d$ being positive semi-definite, where $F_0, \ldots, F_d$ are given symmetric matrices.

nodes.name: Convexity inequality
nodes.statement: $f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y) \leq \lambda f(x) + (1-\lambda) f(y)$

nodes.name: Fourier transform (continuous)
nodes.statement: $f(\omega) = \int x(t) e^{-2\pi \omega t} \, dt$

nodes.name: Inverse Fourier transform (continuous)
nodes.statement: $x(t) = \int f(\omega) e^{2\pi \omega t} \, d\omega$

nodes.name: Discrete Fourier transform entry
nodes.statement: $a_{ij} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega^{ij}$ where $\omega$ is the principal $n$-th root of unity

nodes.name: DFT formula
nodes.statement: $f_j = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} x_k e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{n} j k}$ for $j = 0, \ldots, n-1$

nodes.name: Uncertainty principle bound
nodes.statement: $n_x n_f \geq n$

nodes.name: Second derivative in direction u
nodes.statement: $u^T H(f(x)) u = \sum_{j,i} u_j u_i \frac{\partial^2 f(x)}{\partial x_j \partial x_i}$

nodes.name: Linear program standard form
nodes.statement: $\max c \cdot x$ subject to $Ax = b$, $x \geq 0$

nodes.name: Half-ellipsoid definition
nodes.statement: $E' = \{x : x \in E,\; a \cdot (x - x_0) \geq 0\}$

nodes.name: Ellipsoid volume shrinkage ratio
nodes.statement: $\frac{\mathrm{Vol}(\hat{E})}{\mathrm{Vol}(B)} = \left(\frac{d}{d+1}\right)\left(\frac{d^2}{d^2-1}\right)^{(d-1)/2} \leq 1 - \frac{1}{4d}$

nodes.name: 1-norm minimization reformulation
nodes.statement: $\min \sum_i u_i + \sum_i v_i$ subject to $Au - Av = b$, $u \geq 0$, $v \geq 0$

nodes.name: Incoherence bound on z entries
nodes.statement: $|z_j| < \frac{1}{2s} \|z\|_1$ for every coordinate $j$, unless $z = 0$

nodes.name: Max-cut SDP objective
nodes.statement: $\max \sum_{(i,j) \in E} (1 - y_{ij})$ subject to $Y$ positive semi-definite

nodes.name: Vertex cover LP relaxation
nodes.statement: $\min \sum_i x_i$ subject to $x_i + x_j \geq 1$ for all edges $(i,j)$

nodes.name: Geometric series for spike transform
nodes.statement: $f_b = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{z^{\sqrt{n} b} - 1}{z^b - 1} = 0$ when $b$ is not a multiple of $\sqrt{n}$

nodes.name: Nuclear norm plus sparse decomposition
nodes.statement: $\min \|L\|_* + \lambda \|R\|_1$ subject to $L + R = A$

nodes.name: Extremal position of item ranked first or last
nodes.statement: For rankings where each individual ranks item $b$ either first or last, a global ranking satisfying unanimity and independence of irrelevant alternatives must put $b$ first or last.
assumptions: Each individual ranks $b$ either first or last
Global ranking satisfies unanimity and independence of irrelevant alternatives
conclusions: The global ranking puts $b$ first or last

nodes.statement: Suppose $b$ is not first or last, so $a > b > c$ globally. All individuals can move $c$ above $a$ without affecting the $a,b$ or $b,c$ orders (since $b$ is extreme). By IIA, $a > b > c$ persists, but unanimity forces $c > a$, a contradiction.
Assume for contradiction that $b$ is not first or last in the global ranking; then there exist items $a, c$ with global order $a > b > c$, hence $a > c$ by transitivity.
Since $b$ is first or last on each individual list, every individual can move $c$ above $a$ without changing their relative order of $a,b$ or $b,c$.
By independence of irrelevant alternatives, the global ranking still has $a > b$ and $b > c$ after all individuals move $c$ above $a$.
By unanimity (all individuals now rank $c > a$), the global ranking must put $c > a$, contradicting $a > c$.

nodes.name: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
nodes.statement: Any deterministic algorithm for creating a global ranking from individual rankings of three or more elements satisfying unanimity and independence of irrelevant alternatives is a dictatorship.
assumptions: Satisfies unanimity and independence of irrelevant alternatives
conclusions: The algorithm is a dictatorship: there exists an individual $v$ whose ranking is always the global ranking

nodes.statement: Start with all individuals ranking $b$ last. Move $b$ one-by-one from bottom to top. By Lemma 10.1, when $b$ first moves in the global ranking it jumps to the top. The pivotal individual $v$ is shown to be a dictator for all pairs not involving $b$, then extended to all pairs by repeating for another item $c$.
Start with all individuals ranking $b$ last; by unanimity the global ranking also ranks $b$ last.

Let individuals one by one move $b$ from bottom to top. By unanimity, $b$ must eventually reach the top globally. By Lemma 10.1, when $b$ first moves it jumps all the way to the top. Let $v$ be this pivotal individual.

Show $v$ dictates any pair $a, c$ not involving $b$: consider $v$'s third ranking with $a > b > c$. By IIA, the global ranking has $a > b$ (same $a,b$ votes as before $v$'s switch) and $b > c$ (same $b,c$ votes as after $v$'s switch). By transitivity, global ranking agrees with $v$ on $a > c$.
Other individuals can modify rankings arbitrarily (moving $b$ to any position) without changing the global order of $a$ and $c$, by IIA. So $v$ dictates all pairs not involving $b$.

Repeat the construction for another item $c$. The dictator $v_c$ for pairs not involving $c$ must equal $v$, since both independently control the global ranking of $a$ and $b$. Hence $v$ is a dictator for all pairs.

nodes.name: Unique sparse solution existence
nodes.statement: If $A$ is an $n \times d$ matrix with $n \geq 2s$ and entries chosen from a standard Gaussian, then with probability one $Ax = b$ has a unique $s$-sparse solution. Finding it by brute force takes time $d^s$.
conclusions: With probability one, $Ax = b$ has a unique $s$-sparse solution

nodes.name: Sparse recovery via 1-norm minimization
nodes.statement: If matrix $A$ has unit-length columns $a_1, \ldots, a_d$ with $|a_i \cdot a_j| < 1/(2s)$ for all $i \neq j$, and $Ax = b$ has an $s$-sparse solution, then this solution is the unique minimum 1-norm solution to $Ax = b$.
conclusions: The $s$-sparse solution is the unique minimum $\|x\|_1$ solution to $Ax = b$

nodes.statement: Let $x_0$ be the $s$-sparse solution and $x_1$ the min 1-norm solution. Set $z = x_1 - x_0$. Then $A^T A z = 0$. The near-orthogonality condition implies each $|z_j| < \|z\|_1 / (2s)$. Since $x_1$ minimizes 1-norm, at least half the $\ell_1$ mass of $z$ lies on the support $S$ of $x_0$ ($|S| \leq s$), forcing $\|z\|_1 = 0$.
nodes.proof_strategy: show $z = x_1 - x_0$ must be zero using incoherence and 1-norm optimality

nodes.statement: Let $x_0$ be the $s$-sparse solution, $x_1$ the minimum 1-norm solution, and $z = x_1 - x_0$. Then $Az = 0$, so $A^T A z = 0$.

Since $A^T A$ has ones on the diagonal and off-diagonal entries in $(-1/(2s), 1/(2s))$, the equation $A^T A z = 0$ implies $|z_j| < \frac{1}{2s} \|z\|_1$ for every $j$ (otherwise the $j$-th row of $A^T A z$ cannot be zero).

Let $S$ be the support of $x_0$ with $|S| \leq s$. Let $t_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum_{j \in S} |x_{1,j}|$ and $t_{\mathrm{out}} = \sum_{j \notin S} |x_{1,j}|$. Since $\|x_1\|_1 \leq \|x_0\|_1$, we get $t_0 - t_{\mathrm{in}} \geq t_{\mathrm{out}}$.

Since $\sum_{j \in S} |z_j| \geq t_0 - t_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\sum_{j \notin S} |z_j| = t_{\mathrm{out}}$, at least half the $\ell_1$ mass of $z$ lies in $S$. The average $|z_j|$ for $j \in S$ is at least $\frac{1}{2s}\|z\|_1$, which forces $\|z\|_1 = 0$.

nodes.name: Random matrix sparse recovery
nodes.statement: If $A$ has $n \geq c s^2 \log d$ rows and each column is a random unit-length $n$-dimensional vector, then w.h.p. $A$ satisfies the conditions of Theorem 10.3, and the $s$-sparse solution is recovered by 1-norm minimization.
assumptions: $n \geq c s^2 \log d$ for some constant $c$
Each column of $A$ is a random unit-length $n$-dim vector
conclusions: W.h.p., minimizing $\|x\|_1$ subject to $Ax = b$ recovers the unique $s$-sparse solution

nodes.name: No consecutive zeros in Fourier transform
nodes.statement: If $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}$ has $n_x$ nonzero elements, then its discrete Fourier transform $f_0, \ldots, f_{n-1}$ cannot have $n_x$ consecutive zeros.
conclusions: The Fourier transform of $x$ has no block of $n_x$ consecutive zeros

nodes.statement: Restrict to the $n_x$ nonzero elements and $n_x$ consecutive Fourier coefficients. The resulting matrix is a Vandermonde matrix (after column normalization), which is nonsingular. Since $x \neq 0$, $f \neq 0$.

Let $i_1, \ldots, i_{n_x}$ be the indices of the nonzero elements of $x$. The Fourier coefficients in range $k = m+1, \ldots, m+n_x$ are $f_k = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=1}^{n_x} x_{i_j} e^{-2\pi i k i_j / n}$.
Write $f = Zx$ where $z_{kj} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \exp(-2\pi i k i_j / n)$. The restricted vector $x \neq 0$ by definition.
Rescaling each column of $Z$ by its leading entry yields a Vandermonde matrix, which is nonsingular. Therefore $f = Zx \neq 0$, so there is at least one nonzero Fourier coefficient in the block.

nodes.name: Uncertainty Principle (discrete)
nodes.statement: Let $n_x$ be the number of nonzero elements in $x$ and $n_f$ the number of nonzero elements in its Fourier transform. If $n_x$ divides $n$, then $n_x n_f \geq n$.
assumptions: $x$ is a length-$n$ sequence with $n_x$ nonzero elements
conclusions: $n_x n_f \geq n$ where $n_f$ is the number of nonzero Fourier coefficients

nodes.statement: Since $n_x | n$, partition the Fourier coefficients into $n/n_x$ consecutive blocks of size $n_x$. By Lemma 10.5, each block has at least one nonzero element, so $n_f \geq n/n_x$.
nodes.proof_strategy: partition into blocks and apply Lemma 10.5

nodes.statement: Since $n_x$ divides $n$, partition the $n$ Fourier coefficients into $n / n_x$ consecutive blocks, each of size $n_x$.
By Lemma 10.5, each block of $n_x$ consecutive Fourier coefficients contains at least one nonzero element. Therefore $n_f \geq n / n_x$, i.e., $n_x n_f \geq n$.

nodes.name: Fourier transform of evenly-spaced spikes
nodes.statement: Let $S(\sqrt{n}, \sqrt{n})$ be the sequence of $\sqrt{n}$ ones spaced $\sqrt{n}$ apart. The Fourier transform of $S(\sqrt{n}, \sqrt{n})$ is itself.
assumptions: $S(\sqrt{n}, \sqrt{n})$ is the binary sequence with ones at positions $0, \sqrt{n}, 2\sqrt{n}, \ldots$
conclusions: The discrete Fourier transform of $S(\sqrt{n}, \sqrt{n})$ equals $S(\sqrt{n}, \sqrt{n})$
The bound $n_x n_f \geq n$ in Theorem 10.6 is tight

nodes.statement: For rows indexed $j\sqrt{n}$, the DFT matrix entries at the nonzero columns are all 1, giving $f_{j\sqrt{n}} = 1$ after normalization. For other rows $b$, the entries form a geometric series summing to $(z^{\sqrt{n}b} - 1)/(z^b - 1) = 0$.
nodes.proof_strategy: direct computation using roots of unity

nodes.statement: For row $j\sqrt{n}$ and column $k\sqrt{n}$, the DFT matrix entry is $z^{n k j} = 1$. So the product of these rows with $S(\sqrt{n}, \sqrt{n})$ equals $\sqrt{n}$, and after $1/\sqrt{n}$ normalization, $f_{j\sqrt{n}} = 1$.

For row $b$ not a multiple of $\sqrt{n}$, the entries at nonzero columns are $1, z^b, z^{2b}, \ldots, z^{(\sqrt{n}-1)b}$, a geometric series summing to $(z^{\sqrt{n} b} - 1)/(z^b - 1) = 0$ since $z^{\sqrt{n} b} = 1$ but $z^b \neq 1$.

nodes.name: Gradient descent on convex functions
nodes.statement: If $f$ is a convex, differentiable function on a closed bounded convex domain, then any first-order local minimum is a global minimum. Infinitesimal gradient descent always reaches the global minimum.
assumptions: Domain is closed, bounded, and convex
conclusions: Every first-order local minimum is a global minimum
Infinitesimal gradient descent reaches the global minimum

nodes.statement: If $x$ is a local minimum but not global, let $y$ be a global minimum. By convexity, moving infinitesimally from $x$ toward $y$ decreases $f$, so $\nabla f(x) \neq 0$, contradicting that $x$ is a first-order local minimum.
nodes.proof_strategy: contradiction using convexity along the line to a global minimum

nodes.statement: Assume $x$ is a first-order local minimum but not a global minimum. Let $y \neq x$ be a global minimum with $f(y) < f(x)$.

By convexity, on the line joining $x$ and $y$ the function lies below the line joining $f(x)$ and $f(y)$. For infinitesimal $\epsilon > 0$, moving distance $\epsilon$ from $x$ toward $y$ decreases $f$.
Therefore $\nabla f(x) \neq 0$, contradicting the assumption that $x$ is a first-order local minimum.

nodes.name: Hessian characterization of convexity
nodes.statement: Suppose $f$ maps a closed convex domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ to the reals and the Hessian exists everywhere in $D$. Then $f$ is convex (concave) on $D$ if and only if the Hessian is positive (negative) semi-definite everywhere on $D$.
conclusions: $f$ convex if and only if Hessian is positive semi-definite on $D$
$f$ concave if and only if Hessian is negative semi-definite on $D$

nodes.name: Ellipsoid containing a half-sphere
nodes.statement: The half-sphere $B' = \{x : x_1 \geq 0, |x| \leq 1\}$ is contained in the ellipsoid $\hat{E} = \{x : ((d+1)/d)^2 (x_1 - 1/(d+1))^2 + ((d^2-1)/d^2)(x_2^2 + \cdots + x_d^2) \leq 1\}$, and $\mathrm{Vol}(\hat{E})/\mathrm{Vol}(B) \leq 1 - 1/(4d)$.

nodes.name: LP as special case of SDP
nodes.statement: Linear programs are special cases of semi-definite programs: the constraint $v \geq 0$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{diag}(v)$ being positive semi-definite.
assumptions: Linear program: minimize $c^T x$ subject to $Ax = b$, $x \geq 0$
conclusions: Can be reformulated as an SDP using diagonal matrices

nodes.name: Goemans-Williamson max-cut approximation
nodes.statement: The max-cut problem can be relaxed to an SDP by replacing integer constraints $x_i \in \{-1, +1\}$ with unit vector constraints. Rounding via a random hyperplane yields a cut at least $0.878$ times the maximum.
assumptions: SDP relaxation: maximize $\sum_{(i,j) \in E} (1 - y_{ij})$ with $Y$ positive semi-definite
conclusions: Random hyperplane rounding gives a cut $\geq 0.878 \cdot \mathrm{OPT}$

nodes.name: 1-norm minimization for sparse recovery
nodes.statement: To find the sparse solution to $Ax = b$, minimize $\|x\|_1$ subject to $Ax = b$. Rewrite $x = u - v$, $u, v \geq 0$, and solve the linear program: minimize $\sum_i u_i + \sum_i v_i$ subject to $Au - Av = b$, $u \geq 0$, $v \geq 0$.

nodes.name: Ellipsoid algorithm for linear programming
nodes.statement: Start with a large ball containing the polyhedron $\{x : Ax \leq b\}$. At each step, check if the center is feasible. If not, use a separating hyperplane to find a smaller ellipsoid containing the feasible set. The volume shrinks by factor $1 - 1/(4d)$ per step. Runs in polynomial time.
output: A feasible point $x$ satisfying $Ax \leq b$, or certificate that the system is infeasible
